purpose: Foundational research questions for A* universal architecture function
context_summary: We are defining A*(I, L, K, T): a function from (intent, lifecycle stage, project class, team vector) to a project architecture (folder structure, naming, archival policy, persistence routing). Target: minimize a 9-axis cost vector C = (c_find, c_modify, c_storage, c_money, c_onboard, c_drift, c_reverse, c_loss, c_derive) subject to three integrity constraints (single source of truth, archival reversibility, ontology coherence per folder). Team T splits into T_human, T_agent_internal, T_agent_external. Foundational P0P research. Generalizes S(M,T), the simplicity-times-fit measure used in our routing research.

threads.title: Effective rank and correlation structure of a 9-axis architectural cost vector
threads.input:
I am researching the correlation structure of a 9-dimensional cost vector C used to evaluate software / knowledge project architectures. The 9 axes are: c_find (time to locate an artifact), c_modify (time to change an artifact), c_storage (bytes on disk/cloud), c_money (dollar cost of operating the architecture), c_onboard (time for a new contributor (human or agent) to become productive), c_drift (rate at which architectural integrity decays without intervention), c_reverse (cost of undoing a mistaken operation such as a wrong mv or rm), c_loss (probability per unit time of misplacement, overwrite, orphan, dead link), c_derive (cost of regenerating derived views when a source-of-truth artifact changes).

I need to determine the effective rank of C in practice. A hypothesis from a prior thinking pass is that effective dimensionality is 4-5, with c_find/c_modify clustering and c_storage/c_loss clustering.

Research tasks:

1. Survey the literature that empirically measures correlations among these or analogous cost dimensions. Look across: information retrieval cost models (e.g., Manning + Schutze, IR evaluation literature), software cost models (COCOMO II and successors), software maintenance literature (change coupling, code churn), storage tiering economics (AWS/Google/Azure whitepapers, data temperature literature), archival science (OAIS reference model, PREMIS), developer productivity research (DORA, SPACE framework, GitHub research notes, Microsoft research on developer experience), cognitive load research applied to navigation (Hick's Law and related). For each correlation that the literature supports, cite the source and report the reported correlation or effect size.

2. For each of the 9 axes individually, identify (a) whether literature gives a defensible measurement procedure, (b) the typical units used, (c) the known confounders. If the literature is silent on an axis, say so explicitly.

3. Propose a defensible *upper bound* and *lower bound* on the effective rank of C, with reasoning. Distinguish between (i) the rank if all measurements were perfect, (ii) the rank we can practically estimate from observed projects.

4. Identify which axis pairs literature suggests are most likely to be strongly correlated, and which pairs are most likely to be near-orthogonal.

5. Recommend the minimum data we would need to collect across a portfolio of real projects (e.g., 5-10 software/knowledge repos of varied K) to empirically estimate the rank.

6. Identify any axes that may not be intrinsic to architecture but rather to the team/tooling environment (i.e., axes that should be moved out of C and into a parameter).

Deliverable: a structured research memo with sections matching the 6 tasks above, full citations (URLs where possible), explicit honesty about what the literature does and does not yet support, and a final 'recommended next experiment' section that lists the smallest empirical study that would pin down the rank.

threads.title: Functional-form comparison for A*: continuous optimization vs constraint satisfaction vs constraint optimization
threads.input:
I am choosing a mathematical family for defining A*(I, L, K, T) -> architecture specification. There are three candidate families:

(1) Continuous optimization: classical mathematical programming, multi-objective optimization (weighted sum, epsilon-constraint, lexicographic), evolutionary multi-objective algorithms (NSGA-II, MOEA/D), reinforcement learning.

(2) Constraint satisfaction (CSP): SAT, SMT (Z3, CVC5), answer set programming (Clingo), constraint propagation (Choco, MiniZinc), graph coloring formulations.

(3) Hybrid: constraint optimization problems (COP), weighted CSP, MaxSAT, integer linear programming with side constraints, soft constraint frameworks, neuro-symbolic constraint optimization.

The problem A* solves has these features:

- Hard integrity constraints (single source of truth per fact, archival reversibility, ontology coherence per folder) that must NOT be violated.
- A 9-dimensional cost vector to minimize, with likely effective rank 4-5 due to strong pairwise correlations.
- Parameters (I, L, K, T) where I = intent, L = lifecycle stage, K = project class, T = (T_human, T_agent_internal, T_agent_external).
- Outputs are discrete structural decisions (folder hierarchy, naming scheme, archival policy, persistence routing across multiple stores).
- Solutions must be human-interpretable and human-modifiable (operators need to understand why A* recommended this shape).

Research tasks:

1. For each of the three families, characterize: (a) typical problem formulations that fit our shape, (b) solver maturity and tooling, (c) computational complexity, (d) interpretability of solutions, (e) ease of incremental modification (a 'tune' rather than 're-solve' pattern), (f) ease of incorporating new constraints over time without re-derivation.

2. Survey published applications of each family to *software architecture, folder/file organization, knowledge organization, ontology design, or library science classification*. Cite specific papers. Honestly note where each family has been applied to our exact problem (almost certainly: none directly) versus adjacent problems.

3. For each family, identify the strongest argument against using it for A*, and the strongest argument for.

4. Compare the three families on a structured trade-off table with these columns: hard-constraint enforcement, multi-objective handling, interpretability, incremental tuning, solver maturity for our domain size (5-200 architectural primitives), expected wall-clock to solve, learning curve for an operator (human) to use the framework, learning curve for an agent (script) to query the framework.

5. Discuss recent (2020-) work on neuro-symbolic and constraint optimization, including papers that combine learned heuristics with constraint solvers. Are any of these patterns applicable to A*?

6. Recommend a specific functional form for the v0 of A*, with reasoning. Then recommend the v1 evolution path. Be explicit about what conditions would trigger a v1 redesign.

7. Identify the formal-equivalence relationship between A* and S(M,T) where S(M,T) is a simplicity-times-fit scalar measure: S(M, T) = [Product_j gate_j(M, T)] * [Sum_i w_i * phi_i(M, T)] * exp(-beta * H_i). Show whether S(M,T) is a special case of A* under a specific instantiation (which family in A* generalizes it?), or a sibling construct.

Deliverable: a structured research memo with sections matching the 7 tasks above, full citations (URLs where possible), the trade-off table from task 4, a clear v0 recommendation, and a final 'unanswered questions' section listing what cannot be resolved without empirical work on Buuuk (our v0 testbed).

threads.title: Operational measurement procedures for the 9 cost axes of A*
threads.input:
For each of 9 architectural cost axes, I need to determine a defensible measurement procedure: what to measure, how, with what units, and what confounders to control. The 9 axes:

1. c_find: time for a user (or agent) to locate a specific artifact in the architecture.
2. c_modify: time to apply a planned change to an artifact (including locating dependencies and updating them).
3. c_storage: bytes on disk and cloud occupied by the architecture (including derived views and archives).
4. c_money: dollar cost of operating the architecture per unit time (storage fees, API call fees for persistence layers, CI/CD costs attributable to architecture).
5. c_onboard: time for a new contributor (human or AI agent) to become productive in the architecture (a measurable definition of 'productive' is required).
6. c_drift: rate at which architectural integrity decays without active intervention. Measurable as drift in some integrity score over time.
7. c_reverse: cost (time + risk) of undoing a mistaken operation (a wrong file move, deletion, rename, or restructure).
8. c_loss: probability per unit time of misplacement, overwrite, orphan, or dead-link events affecting any artifact.
9. c_derive: cost of regenerating derived views (caches, indexes, embeddings, summaries) when a source-of-truth artifact changes.

Research tasks per axis:

For each of the 9 axes, return:
(a) The published measurement procedures the literature offers (cite specific papers, frameworks, or industry standards). Mark each citation with the field it comes from: IR, software engineering, knowledge management, archival science, developer experience research, cloud economics, etc.
(b) Proposed units (e.g., seconds-per-task, bytes, USD-per-month, probability-per-week, etc.).
(c) Known confounders that must be controlled for in real measurement.
(d) Whether the axis is measurable as written (LITERATURE), needs adaptation from an adjacent literature (HYBRID), or requires fresh invention (INVENT).
(e) If INVENT or HYBRID: a proposed measurement procedure with explicit limitations.
(f) Rank the axis on measurement difficulty (1 = trivial, 5 = research-grade).

Additional tasks:

10. Identify any of the 9 axes where the literature suggests the metric is fundamentally non-measurable or only measurable in retrospect (e.g., maybe c_drift can only be measured after the fact). Discuss.

11. Identify proxies that can be measured cheaply at sub-architecture granularity (per-folder, per-file) and aggregated to architecture-level. Tree-level structural metrics (depth, branching factor, entropy) are obvious candidates; survey what is known about their correlation with the 9 axes.

12. Identify *passive* measurement strategies that can be applied to an existing repo without instrumenting users (e.g., parsing git log, scanning filesystem stats, parsing CI logs). Distinguish from *active* measurement (requires user studies).

13. Recommend a minimum-viable measurement instrument: a tool we could build that estimates all 9 c_i for an arbitrary repo using passive signals only. List the inputs the tool would need.

Deliverable: a structured research memo with a 9-row table covering tasks (a)-(f), followed by sections for tasks 10-13, with full citations (URLs where possible), and a final 'measurement risks' section listing the c_i where measurement uncertainty is highest.
